## 17.18 Deployment advisory

```text
[ ] Mutate concrete instances only.
[ ] For AbstractModel, call create_instance(...) once, then mutate instance.
[ ] Use mutable Params for repeated numeric data changes.
[ ] Use Var.fix/unfix for forced decisions.
[ ] Use setlb/setub for bound changes.
[ ] Use ConstraintList for iterative cuts/no-good constraints.
[ ] Use activate/deactivate for reversible known constraints/objectives.
[ ] Use objective set_value/expr mutation for objective sweeps.
[ ] Use load_solutions=False and termination checks in every loop.
[ ] Treat previous solution values as warm starts after mutation, not final values.
[ ] Rebuild model when index sets/variable dimensions change.
[ ] Consider APPSI/persistent solvers for high-frequency repeated related solves.
[ ] If using persistent solvers, explicitly notify solver of add/remove/update operations.
[ ] Add regression tests for each mutation path.
```

---

## 17.19 Anti-pattern table

| Anti-pattern                                                  | Failure mode                | Replacement                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| mutate `AbstractModel` template                               | solved instance unchanged   | mutate `instance`                            |
| assign to immutable `Param`                                   | error                       | declare `mutable=True`                       |
| use `pyo.value(mutable_param)` inside constraint              | frozen value                | use symbolic `Param`                         |
| report values after mutation without re-solve                 | stale report                | re-solve and load                            |
| add many known static rows via `ConstraintList`               | poor structure/reporting    | indexed `Constraint`                         |
| use dense skip loop for cuts                                  | slow construction           | sparse cut/index support                     |
| fix variable when intending warm start                        | variable cannot move        | `set_value(...)`                             |
| set equal bounds while variable remains fixed elsewhere       | bounds ignored              | `unfix()` or use `fix(...)` intentionally    |
| replace persistent-solver constraint without removing old one | extra stale solver-side row | `remove_constraint`, `del_component`, re-add |
| multiple active objectives after switching                    | solver/export ambiguity     | deactivate inactive objectives               |
| changing index sets after variables/constraints exist         | inconsistent structure      | rebuild model                                |
| accepting nonoptimal loop termination silently                | bad algorithm state         | classify termination explicitly              |

---

## 17.20 Agent-ready production template

```python
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any, Callable

import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pyomo.opt import SolverStatus, TerminationCondition


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SolverConfig:
    name: str = "highs"
    options: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)
    tee: bool = False
    acceptable_terminations: frozenset = frozenset({
        TerminationCondition.optimal,
    })


def solve_checked(model: pyo.ConcreteModel, cfg: SolverConfig):
    opt = pyo.SolverFactory(cfg.name)

    if opt is None or not opt.available(exception_flag=False):
        raise RuntimeError(f"solver unavailable: {cfg.name}")

    results = opt.solve(
        model,
        options=cfg.options,
        tee=cfg.tee,
        load_solutions=False,
    )

    if (
        results.solver.status == SolverStatus.ok
        and results.solver.termination_condition in cfg.acceptable_terminations
    ):
        model.solutions.load_from(results)
        return results

    raise RuntimeError(
        f"bad solve: status={results.solver.status}, "
        f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"
    )


def clear_import_suffixes(model: pyo.Block) -> None:
    for suffix_name in ("dual", "rc", "slack"):
        if hasattr(model, suffix_name):
            getattr(model, suffix_name).clearAllValues()


def mark_nonfixed_variables_stale(model: pyo.Block) -> None:
    for v in model.component_data_objects(pyo.Var, active=True, descend_into=True):
        if not v.fixed:
            v.stale = True


def mutate_then_solve(
    model: pyo.ConcreteModel,
    mutation: Callable[[pyo.ConcreteModel], None],
    cfg: SolverConfig,
):
    mutation(model)
    clear_import_suffixes(model)
    mark_nonfixed_variables_stale(model)
    return solve_checked(model, cfg)


def add_no_good_cut(model: pyo.ConcreteModel, binary_var: pyo.Var) -> None:
    if not hasattr(model, "no_good_cuts"):
        model.no_good_cuts = pyo.ConstraintList()

    expr = 0
    for idx in binary_var:
        val = pyo.value(binary_var[idx])
        if val is None:
            raise ValueError(f"binary variable has no value: {binary_var[idx].name}")
        expr += binary_var[idx] if val < 0.5 else 1 - binary_var[idx]

    model.no_good_cuts.add(expr >= 1)


def update_mutable_param(param, values) -> None:
    if param.is_indexed():
        valid = set(param.keys())
        extra = set(values) - valid
        if extra:
            raise KeyError(f"unknown Param indices: {sorted(extra)[:20]}")
        for idx, val in values.items():
            param[idx] = val
    else:
        param.set_value(values)


def fix_variables(var, values: dict) -> None:
    valid = set(var.keys()) if var.is_indexed() else {None}

    if var.is_indexed():
        extra = set(values) - valid
        if extra:
            raise KeyError(f"unknown Var indices: {sorted(extra)[:20]}")
        for idx, val in values.items():
            var[idx].fix(val)
    else:
        var.fix(values)


def unfix_variables(var) -> None:
    if var.is_indexed():
        for idx in var:
            var[idx].unfix()
    else:
        var.unfix()


def update_bounds(var, lb=None, ub=None) -> None:
    if var.is_indexed():
        for idx in var:
            if lb is not None:
                var[idx].setlb(lb[idx] if isinstance(lb, dict) else lb)
            if ub is not None:
                var[idx].setub(ub[idx] if isinstance(ub, dict) else ub)
    else:
        if lb is not None:
            var.setlb(lb)
        if ub is not None:
            var.setub(ub)


def switch_objective(model: pyo.Block, objective_name: str) -> None:
    for obj in model.component_objects(pyo.Objective, active=True, descend_into=True):
        obj.deactivate()

    obj = model.find_component(objective_name)
    if obj is None:
        raise KeyError(f"objective not found: {objective_name}")

    obj.activate()


def require_single_active_objective(model: pyo.Block):
    objs = list(model.component_data_objects(pyo.Objective, active=True, descend_into=True))
    if len(objs) != 1:
        raise RuntimeError(f"expected one active objective, found {len(objs)}")
    return objs[0]


def repeated_rhs_sweep(model: pyo.ConcreteModel, rhs_values, cfg: SolverConfig):
    out = []

    for rhs in rhs_values:
        def mutation(m):
            m.rhs = rhs

        mutate_then_solve(model, mutation, cfg)

        obj = require_single_active_objective(model)
        out.append({
            "rhs": rhs,
            "objective": pyo.value(obj),
            "variables": {
                v.name: pyo.value(v, exception=False)
                for v in model.component_data_objects(pyo.Var, active=True, descend_into=True)
            },
        })

    return out


def enumerate_binary_solutions(
    model: pyo.ConcreteModel,
    binary_var: pyo.Var,
    cfg: SolverConfig,
    max_solutions: int = 20,
):
    solutions = []

    for k in range(max_solutions):
        solve_checked(model, cfg)

        sol = {
            idx: round(pyo.value(binary_var[idx]))
            for idx in binary_var
        }
        solutions.append(sol)

        add_no_good_cut(model, binary_var)
        clear_import_suffixes(model)
        mark_nonfixed_variables_stale(model)

    return solutions
```

---

## 17.21 Final checklist

```text
[ ] Apply model manipulations to ConcreteModel or instantiated AbstractModel instance.
[ ] Use ConstraintList.add(...) for dynamic cuts.
[ ] Use mutable=True Params for repeated numeric updates.
[ ] Use Var.fix(value) / Var.unfix() for forced decisions.
[ ] Use Var.setlb(...) / Var.setub(...) for bound updates.
[ ] Use Objective.expr / set_value(...) for objective mutation.
[ ] Use activate/deactivate for reversible constraints/objectives.
[ ] Use del_component/re-add only for structural replacement.
[ ] Use load_solutions=False inside repeated solve loops.
[ ] Check termination before loading and before using pyo.value(...).
[ ] Clear imported suffixes before repeated solves.
[ ] Mark or treat old variable values as stale after mutation.
[ ] Rebuild when index sets or variable dimensions change.
[ ] Prefer APPSI/persistent solvers for many small related updates after correctness is proven.
[ ] With persistent solvers, notify solver explicitly of add/remove/update operations.
[ ] Unit-test every mutation path.
```

[1]: https://pyomo.readthedocs.io/en/6.8.2/howto/manipulating.html "Manipulating Pyomo Models — Pyomo 6.8.2 documentation"
[2]: https://pyomo.readthedocs.io/en/stable/explanation/solvers/persistent.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Persistent Solvers - Pyomo Documentation 6.10.0"
[3]: https://pyomo.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/topical/appsi/appsi.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com "APPSI - Pyomo Documentation 6.10.0"

# 18) Persistent solvers and APPSI — Pyomo deep dive

Style target: uploaded advanced technical-doc plan. 

Persistent solver interfaces maintain a **live solver-side model** corresponding to a Pyomo model. Pyomo’s persistent-solver docs state the purpose is to efficiently notify the solver of incremental model changes instead of recreating the full model through the solver API or rewriting an entire solver file each solve; for example, `GurobiPersistent` maintains a pointer to a `gurobipy.Model`. The same docs warn that users are responsible for notifying persistent solver interfaces when Pyomo model changes are made. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

---

## 18.0 Mental model

```text id="7wqbri"
Classic file/direct SolverFactory:
  each solve(model) exports or rebuilds current Pyomo state
  easy correctness model
  slower for many small repeated updates

Classic persistent solver:
  set_instance(model) creates solver-side model once
  Pyomo model and solver-side model can diverge
  user must call add/remove/update methods
  very efficient when updates are small and tracked correctly

APPSI:
  Auto-Persistent Pyomo Solver Interfaces
  designed to behave like normal Pyomo solver interfaces
  efficient for resolving same model with small changes
  can auto-check/update model changes according to update_config
```

Primary use cases:

```text id="l8b9az"
Benders decomposition
outer approximation
optimization-based bounds tightening
progressive hedging
column/row generation variants
parametric sweeps
rolling horizon
MPC-style repeated solves
large model + small changes
```

Pyomo’s APPSI docs identify Benders decomposition, optimization-based bounds tightening, progressive hedging, outer approximation, and related algorithms as motivating applications for efficient repeated solves of the same model with small changes. ([Pyomo Documentation][2])

---

## 18.1 Classic persistent solvers vs APPSI

| Feature               | Classic persistent                            | APPSI                                                               |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Access route          | `pyo.SolverFactory("gurobi_persistent")`      | `from pyomo.contrib import appsi` or `SolverFactory("appsi_highs")` |
| Model loading         | `opt.set_instance(model)`                     | `opt.solve(model)` can auto-set/update                              |
| Update responsibility | explicit user notifications                   | auto-persistent update machinery, configurable                      |
| Update tuning         | solver-specific methods                       | `update_config` flags                                               |
| Result object         | classic Pyomo results-ish                     | APPSI `Results` / `TerminationCondition`                            |
| Best fit              | expert solver scripting, direct native access | repeated solves with easier persistent semantics                    |
| Risk                  | Pyomo/solver divergence if updates missed     | performance/correctness depends on update config                    |

APPSI currently documents solvers for **Gurobi, Ipopt, Cplex, Cbc, HiGHS, and MAiNGO**, and APPSI interfaces can also be accessed through classic `SolverFactory` using names such as `appsi_ipopt` and `appsi_highs`. ([Pyomo Documentation][2])

---

## 18.2 Classic persistent solver names

Typical names:

```python id="z9d0oi"
pyo.SolverFactory("gurobi_persistent")
pyo.SolverFactory("cplex_persistent")
pyo.SolverFactory("xpress_persistent")
pyo.SolverFactory("mosek_persistent")
```

Availability varies by installed Pyomo plugins, solver Python packages, licenses, and Pyomo version.

Production probe:

```python id="e4qxyk"
import pyomo.environ as pyo

def require_classic_persistent_solver(name: str):
    opt = pyo.SolverFactory(name)

    if opt is None or not opt.available(exception_flag=False):
        raise RuntimeError(f"persistent solver unavailable: {name}")

    if hasattr(opt, "license_is_valid"):
        try:
            if not opt.license_is_valid():
                raise RuntimeError(f"solver license invalid: {name}")
        except NotImplementedError:
            pass

    return opt
```

---

## 18.3 Classic persistent workflow

### 18.3.1 Build normal Pyomo model

```python id="mzwdcl"
import pyomo.environ as pyo

m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
m.x = pyo.Var()
m.y = pyo.Var()

m.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=m.x**2 + m.y**2)
m.c = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.y >= -2 * m.x + 5)
```

### 18.3.2 Create persistent solver

```python id="v4zyue"
opt = pyo.SolverFactory("gurobi_persistent")
```

### 18.3.3 Attach model

```python id="z0hjj7"
opt.set_instance(m)
```

`set_instance(m)` creates the solver-native model and includes the corresponding variables and constraints. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

### 18.3.4 Solve

```python id="bs16c1"
results = opt.solve()
```

### 18.3.5 Load values

```python id="1pqyft"
opt.load_vars()
```

Classic persistent solvers support loading primal variable values from the solver into the Pyomo variables; persistent-solver performance docs show `opt.load_vars()` after `solve(save_results=False, load_solutions=False)`, and also show loading a subset such as `opt.load_vars(m.x)`. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

---

## 18.4 Classic persistent update primitives

### 18.4.1 Add constraint

```python id="s0jq6e"
m.c2 = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.y >= m.x)
opt.add_constraint(m.c2)
results = opt.solve()
```

The persistent solver docs show adding a new Pyomo constraint, then calling `opt.add_constraint(m.c2)` to add only that new row to the solver-side model before resolving. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

### 18.4.2 Remove constraint

```python id="duwq70"
opt.remove_constraint(m.c2)
del m.c2
results = opt.solve()
```

Pyomo docs show removing a component from the solver first, then deleting it from the Pyomo model. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

### 18.4.3 Replace constraint safely

Wrong:

```python id="6nnl6w"
del m.c
m.c = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.y <= m.x)
opt.add_constraint(m.c)
```

Correct:

```python id="i1jzxi"
opt.remove_constraint(m.c)
del m.c

m.c = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.y <= m.x)
opt.add_constraint(m.c)
```

If a Pyomo component is replaced with another component of the same name, the first component must be removed from the solver or the solver-side model can contain both the old and new components; Pyomo’s docs explicitly mark the delete-then-add pattern without `remove_constraint` as wrong. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

### 18.4.4 Update variable bounds / type / fixed status

```python id="au4ilj"
m.x.setlb(1.0)
opt.update_var(m.x)
```

Persistent docs state that, in most cases, modifying a component requires removing it from the solver instance, modifying it in Pyomo, and adding it back; the exception is variables, which may be modified and then updated with the solver using `update_var`. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

### 18.4.5 Add/remove variables

```python id="51bs95"
m.z = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)
opt.add_var(m.z)

opt.remove_var(m.z)
del m.z
```

### 18.4.6 Add/remove block

```python id="oh5rml"
m.b = pyo.Block()
m.b.x = pyo.Var()
m.b.c = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.b.x >= 0)

opt.add_block(m.b)

opt.remove_block(m.b)
del m.b
```

Caution: removing a block after adding a new constraint to the block without adding that new constraint to the solver can error because the solver does not know that component. Pyomo’s docs show this exact failure mode and warn that components removed from a Pyomo model must be removed from the solver instance by the user. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

---

## 18.5 Indexed variables and constraints in classic persistent solvers

### 18.5.1 Add indexed variable correctly

```python id="fh65l5"
for v in indexed_var.values():
    opt.add_var(v)
```

### 18.5.2 Add indexed constraint correctly

```python id="tslf95"
for c in indexed_con.values():
    opt.add_constraint(c)
```

### 18.5.3 Generic helper

```python id="l1jeqm"
def add_variable(opt, var):
    if var.is_indexed():
        for v in var.values():
            opt.add_var(v)
    else:
        opt.add_var(var)


def add_constraint(opt, con):
    if con.is_indexed():
        for c in con.values():
            opt.add_constraint(c)
    else:
        opt.add_constraint(con)
```

Pyomo’s persistent docs state that indexed variables/constraints must be iterated over with `.values()` when adding/removing; passing an `IndexedVar` directly can raise errors such as `'IndexedVar' object has no attribute 'is_binary'`, and passing an indexed constraint directly can fail because an `IndexedConstraint` has no `.body`. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

---

## 18.6 Classic persistent performance mode

### 18.6.1 `save_results=False`

```python id="56t31m"
results = opt.solve(save_results=False)
```

### 18.6.2 Load variables after solve

```python id="902hic"
results = opt.solve(save_results=False, load_solutions=False)

if results.solver.termination_condition == pyo.TerminationCondition.optimal:
    opt.load_vars()
```

### 18.6.3 Load subset

```python id="20a6ke"
opt.load_vars(m.x)
```

Pyomo’s persistent performance docs recommend `save_results=False` for best persistent-solver performance and state that when `save_results=False`, the normal `model.solutions.load_from(results)` pathway is not supported; use `opt.load_vars()` or `opt.load_vars(m.x)` instead. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

---

## 18.7 Classic persistent no-good cut loop

```python id="aeqntx"
def enumerate_binary_solutions_persistent(model, binary_var, solver_name="gurobi_persistent", max_solutions=20):
    opt = pyo.SolverFactory(solver_name)
    opt.set_instance(model)

    if not hasattr(model, "cuts"):
        model.cuts = pyo.ConstraintList()

    solutions = []

    for k in range(max_solutions):
        results = opt.solve(save_results=False, load_solutions=False)
        if results.solver.termination_condition != pyo.TerminationCondition.optimal:
            break

        opt.load_vars()

        sol = {idx: round(pyo.value(binary_var[idx])) for idx in binary_var}
        solutions.append(sol)

        expr = 0
        for idx, val in sol.items():
            expr += binary_var[idx] if val == 0 else 1 - binary_var[idx]

        new_cut = model.cuts.add(expr >= 1)
        opt.add_constraint(new_cut)

    return solutions
```

Key persistent detail:

```text id="npnpfh"
ConstraintList.add(...) changes Pyomo model only.
opt.add_constraint(new_cut) is required to update solver-side model.
```

---

## 18.8 Classic persistent bound-update loop

```python id="ilnm3v"
def bound_sweep_persistent(model, bounds_by_case, solver_name="gurobi_persistent"):
    opt = pyo.SolverFactory(solver_name)
    opt.set_instance(model)

    out = []

    for case_name, bounds in bounds_by_case.items():
        for idx, (lb, ub) in bounds.items():
            model.x[idx].setlb(lb)
            model.x[idx].setub(ub)
            opt.update_var(model.x[idx])

        results = opt.solve(save_results=False, load_solutions=False)
        if results.solver.termination_condition == pyo.TerminationCondition.optimal:
            opt.load_vars(model.x)
            out.append({
                "case": case_name,
                "objective": pyo.value(model.obj),
                "x": {idx: pyo.value(model.x[idx]) for idx in model.x},
            })

    return out
```

---

## 18.9 Classic persistent objective replacement

Pattern:

```python id="9p8th5"
m.obj.deactivate()
m.obj2 = pyo.Objective(expr=new_expr)
opt.set_objective(m.obj2)
```

or, depending on classic persistent solver interface:

```python id="9t8mbg"
m.obj.set_value(new_expr)
opt.set_objective(m.obj)
```

Deployment note:

```text id="vblbwz"
Classic persistent objective update APIs vary by interface.
Prefer a tested helper per solver.
If uncertain, remove/re-set full instance or use APPSI.
```

## 18.10 APPSI basic workflow

### 18.10.1 Import APPSI

```python id="4myuiu"
import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pyomo.contrib import appsi
```

### 18.10.2 Create model

```python id="fzgbwa"
m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
m.x = pyo.Var()
m.y = pyo.Var()
m.p = pyo.Param(mutable=True)

m.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=m.x**2 + m.y**2)
m.c1 = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.y >= pyo.exp(m.x))
m.c2 = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.y >= (m.x - m.p)**2)
```

### 18.10.3 Solve repeatedly

```python id="kgm9qr"
opt = appsi.solvers.Ipopt()

for p_val in range(1, 11):
    m.p.value = float(p_val)
    res = opt.solve(m)
    assert res.termination_condition == appsi.base.TerminationCondition.optimal
    print(res.best_feasible_objective)
```

Pyomo’s APPSI example shows `appsi.solvers.Ipopt()` resolving the same model for a sequence of mutable parameter values, with termination checked against `appsi.base.TerminationCondition.optimal`. ([Pyomo Documentation][2])

### 18.10.4 Access APPSI through `SolverFactory`

```python id="2ychq6"
opt_ipopt = pyo.SolverFactory("appsi_ipopt")
opt_highs = pyo.SolverFactory("appsi_highs")
```

APPSI docs show this exact access pattern. ([Pyomo Documentation][2])

## 18.13 APPSI loading and data access

### 18.13.1 Direct solve updates model values

```python id="1ct96i"
res = opt.solve(m)
print(pyo.value(m.x))
```

### 18.13.2 Persistent API methods

APPSI `PersistentSolver` exposes methods including:

```text id="6u69c2"
set_instance(model)
add_variables(...)
add_constraints(...)
add_params(...)
add_block(...)
remove_variables(...)
remove_constraints(...)
remove_params(...)
remove_block(...)
set_objective(obj)
update_variables(...)
update_params()
load_vars(...)
get_primals(...)
get_duals(...)
get_reduced_costs(...)
get_slacks(...)
```

The APPSI `PersistentSolver` API lists these methods and documents `load_vars` as loading primal variable values into Pyomo variable `.value` attributes. ([Pyomo Documentation][3])

### 18.13.3 Duals/reduced costs/slacks through APPSI

```python id="cvl9kz"
duals = opt.get_duals()
rc = opt.get_reduced_costs()
slacks = opt.get_slacks()
primals = opt.get_primals()
```

Use only when solver/interface supports them.

## 18.14 APPSI update configuration

### 18.14.1 Parameter-only repeated solve tuning

```python id="7dnsr1"
opt.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_constraints = False
opt.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_vars = False
opt.update_config.update_constraints = False
opt.update_config.update_vars = False
```

APPSI docs show exactly this tuning when only mutable parameter values change, allowing the solver to skip checks for new/removed variables/constraints and skip variable/constraint updates. ([Pyomo Documentation][2])

### 18.14.2 Available common flags

```python id="wzwsb0"
opt.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_constraints
opt.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_vars
opt.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_params
opt.update_config.update_constraints
opt.update_config.update_vars
opt.update_config.update_params
opt.update_config.update_named_expressions
```

`UpdateConfig` is documented as common to persistent solvers and includes flags for checking new/removed constraints, variables, and parameters, plus updating constraints, variables, parameters, and named expressions. ([Pyomo Documentation][4])

### 18.14.3 Configuration safety rule

```text id="j9w4kt"
Only disable update checks when you can prove the corresponding structure does not change.
Wrong update_config can produce stale solver-side models.
```

### 18.14.4 Safe defaults

```text id="weonb0"
Development:
  leave update_config defaults alone
  prioritize correctness

Production parameter sweeps:
  disable checks/updates only for categories guaranteed unchanged
  add regression tests proving same results as full-update configuration
```

---

## 18.15 APPSI solver options

### 18.15.1 Solver-independent config

```python id="t771l7"
opt.config.stream_solver = True
```

### 18.15.2 Solver-specific options

```python id="zmzt16"
opt.solver_options["max_iter"] = 20
```

APPSI docs distinguish solver-independent options via `config` or derived config classes from solver-specific options through `solver_options`. ([Pyomo Documentation][2])

### 18.15.3 Example: HiGHS

```python id="07nhuw"
opt = appsi.solvers.Highs()
opt.config.stream_solver = True
opt.solver_options["time_limit"] = 300
opt.solver_options["mip_rel_gap"] = 1e-4
res = opt.solve(m)
```

### 18.15.4 Example: Ipopt

```python id="y4wa88"
opt = appsi.solvers.Ipopt()
opt.config.stream_solver = True
opt.solver_options["max_iter"] = 3000
opt.solver_options["tol"] = 1e-7
res = opt.solve(m)
```

## 18.16 APPSI availability

```python id="7m5dsh"
availability = opt.available()

if not bool(availability):
    raise RuntimeError(f"solver unavailable: {availability}")
```

APPSI `Solver.available()` returns an availability enum; docs state it can represent levels such as available with limitations for licensed solvers or failure categories such as not found, bad license, and unsupported version, and it casts to bool for runnable/non-runnable status. ([Pyomo Documentation][3])

## 18.17 APPSI parameter sweep template

```python id="n8npbu"
import numpy as np
import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pyomo.contrib import appsi


def build_model():
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
    m.x = pyo.Var(initialize=1.0)
    m.y = pyo.Var(initialize=1.0)
    m.p = pyo.Param(mutable=True, initialize=1.0)

    m.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=m.x**2 + m.y**2)
    m.c1 = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.y >= pyo.exp(m.x))
    m.c2 = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.y >= (m.x - m.p)**2)

    return m


m = build_model()
opt = appsi.solvers.Ipopt()

# Safe after verified parameter-only updates.
opt.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_constraints = False
opt.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_vars = False
opt.update_config.update_constraints = False
opt.update_config.update_vars = False

out = []

for p_val in np.linspace(1, 10, 100):
    m.p.value = float(p_val)
    res = opt.solve(m)

    if res.termination_condition != appsi.base.TerminationCondition.optimal:
        raise RuntimeError(res.termination_condition)

    out.append({
        "p": float(p_val),
        "objective": res.best_feasible_objective,
        "x": pyo.value(m.x),
        "y": pyo.value(m.y),
    })
```

## 18.18 APPSI OBBT-style objective loop

```python id="oywzpj"
def obbt_appsi(model, variables, opt):
    original_obj = next(model.component_data_objects(pyo.Objective, active=True))
    original_obj.deactivate()

    model._obbt_obj = pyo.Objective(expr=0.0)

    bounds = {}

    for v in variables:
        model._obbt_obj.set_value(v)
        model._obbt_obj.sense = pyo.minimize
        res = opt.solve(model)

        if res.termination_condition == appsi.base.TerminationCondition.optimal:
            lb = pyo.value(v)
        else:
            lb = None

        model._obbt_obj.sense = pyo.maximize
        res = opt.solve(model)

        if res.termination_condition == appsi.base.TerminationCondition.optimal:
            ub = pyo.value(v)
        else:
            ub = None

        bounds[v.name] = (lb, ub)

        if lb is not None:
            v.setlb(max(v.lb if v.lb is not None else lb, lb))
        if ub is not None:
            v.setub(min(v.ub if v.ub is not None else ub, ub))

    model._obbt_obj.deactivate()
    original_obj.activate()

    return bounds
```

Update-config note:

```text id="snrrki"
Objective and variable-bound changes occur here.
Do not disable update_vars or objective-related updates unless tested.
```

## 18.19 Classic persistent vs APPSI selection matrix

| Need                                          |        Classic persistent |                             APPSI |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------: | --------------------------------: |
| Direct access to native Gurobi/CPLEX model    |                    strong |                   solver-specific |
| Expert manual add/remove/update control       |                    strong |  possible through persistent APIs |
| Easy repeated parameter sweeps                |                  possible |                            strong |
| Automatic update detection                    |         weak/user-managed |               strong/configurable |
| Fine-grained solver-side manipulation         |                    strong |                  solver-dependent |
| Consistent APPSI result object                |                        no |                               yes |
| High safety for novice agents                 |                     lower | higher with default update config |
| Maximum performance with known update pattern |                    strong | strong with tuned `update_config` |
| Many structural edits                         | possible, but error-prone |       possible with update checks |
| Existing code using `gurobi_persistent`       |                       yes |                  migration needed |

Agent default:

```text id="jftq5w"
Use classic SolverFactory first for correctness.
Use APPSI for repeated solves with small changes.
Use classic persistent when native solver object access or manual solver-side control is required.
```

---

## 18.20 Persistent solver state hazards

### 18.20.1 Pyomo and solver-side model divergence

```text id="6bibnn"
Pyomo model changed:
  solver-side model unchanged until notification/update

Solver-side model changed:
  Pyomo model may not reflect native modifications unless loaded/synchronized
```

### 18.20.2 Component replacement hazard

```python id="zhtpga"
# WRONG
del m.c
m.c = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.y <= m.x)
opt.add_constraint(m.c)
```

Outcome:

```text id="sktcqc"
solver may retain old c and add new c
model and solver diverge
```

Correct:

```python id="bna23o"
opt.remove_constraint(m.c)
del m.c
m.c = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.y <= m.x)
opt.add_constraint(m.c)
```

Pyomo docs explicitly show this as the correct replacement sequence. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

### 18.20.3 ConstraintList hazard

```python id="dck5gf"
new_con = m.cuts.add(expr >= 1)
# Must also:
opt.add_constraint(new_con)
```

### 18.20.4 Indexed component hazard

```python id="fzaj6a"
# WRONG
opt.add_constraint(m.con)
```

Correct:

```python id="60qo8p"
for c in m.con.values():
    opt.add_constraint(c)
```

Pyomo docs show direct `opt.add_constraint(indexed_con)` as erroneous because indexed containers do not expose leaf constraint attributes like `.body`; iterate `.values()`. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

---

## 18.21 Persistent helper layer

```python id="cg77w8"
def _iter_component_data(comp):
    if comp.is_indexed():
        yield from comp.values()
    else:
        yield comp


def persistent_add_var(opt, var):
    for v in _iter_component_data(var):
        opt.add_var(v)


def persistent_remove_var(opt, var):
    for v in _iter_component_data(var):
        opt.remove_var(v)


def persistent_add_constraint(opt, con):
    for c in _iter_component_data(con):
        opt.add_constraint(c)


def persistent_remove_constraint(opt, con):
    for c in _iter_component_data(con):
        opt.remove_constraint(c)


def persistent_update_var(opt, var):
    for v in _iter_component_data(var):
        opt.update_var(v)
```

Use:

```python id="5i761t"
m.x = pyo.Var(m.I)
persistent_add_var(opt, m.x)

m.c = pyo.Constraint(m.I, rule=rule)
persistent_add_constraint(opt, m.c)
```

## 18.22 Persistent solve wrapper

```python id="ewy91g"
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any

import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pyomo.opt import TerminationCondition


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PersistentConfig:
    solver_name: str = "gurobi_persistent"
    options: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)
    save_results: bool = False
    tee: bool = False


def make_persistent_solver(model: pyo.ConcreteModel, cfg: PersistentConfig):
    opt = pyo.SolverFactory(cfg.solver_name)

    if opt is None or not opt.available(exception_flag=False):
        raise RuntimeError(f"solver unavailable: {cfg.solver_name}")

    opt.set_instance(model)

    for key, value in cfg.options.items():
        opt.options[key] = value

    return opt


def solve_persistent_checked(opt, model, cfg: PersistentConfig):
    results = opt.solve(
        save_results=cfg.save_results,
        load_solutions=False,
        tee=cfg.tee,
    )

    if results.solver.termination_condition == TerminationCondition.optimal:
        if cfg.save_results:
            model.solutions.load_from(results)
        else:
            opt.load_vars()
        return results

    raise RuntimeError(f"bad termination: {results.solver.termination_condition}")
```

Note:

```text id="my2gmk"
If save_results=False, use opt.load_vars() instead of model.solutions.load_from(results).
```

This follows Pyomo persistent performance docs. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

## 18.23 APPSI solve wrapper

```python id="335742"
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any

import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pyomo.contrib import appsi


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AppsiConfig:
    solver: str = "highs"
    stream_solver: bool = False
    solver_options: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)
    parameter_only_updates: bool = False


def make_appsi_solver(cfg: AppsiConfig):
    if cfg.solver == "highs":
        opt = appsi.solvers.Highs()
    elif cfg.solver == "ipopt":
        opt = appsi.solvers.Ipopt()
    elif cfg.solver == "gurobi":
        opt = appsi.solvers.Gurobi()
    elif cfg.solver == "cplex":
        opt = appsi.solvers.Cplex()
    elif cfg.solver == "cbc":
        opt = appsi.solvers.Cbc()
    elif cfg.solver == "maingo":
        opt = appsi.solvers.MAiNGO()
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown APPSI solver: {cfg.solver}")

    if not bool(opt.available()):
        raise RuntimeError(f"APPSI solver unavailable: {cfg.solver}: {opt.available()}")

    opt.config.stream_solver = cfg.stream_solver

    for key, value in cfg.solver_options.items():
        opt.solver_options[key] = value

    if cfg.parameter_only_updates:
        opt.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_constraints = False
        opt.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_vars = False
        opt.update_config.update_constraints = False
        opt.update_config.update_vars = False

    return opt


def solve_appsi_checked(opt, model):
    res = opt.solve(model)

    if res.termination_condition != appsi.base.TerminationCondition.optimal:
        raise RuntimeError(f"bad termination: {res.termination_condition}")

    return res
```

## 18.25 Regression tests for persistent correctness

### 18.25.1 Compare classic vs persistent after mutation

```python id="vqy0du"
def solve_classic(model):
    opt = pyo.SolverFactory("highs")
    res = opt.solve(model)
    return pyo.value(model.obj)


def test_persistent_matches_classic_after_bound_update(sample_model):
    m1 = sample_model.clone()
    m2 = sample_model.clone()

    # classic
    m1.x.setlb(1.0)
    obj_classic = solve_classic(m1)

    # persistent
    opt = pyo.SolverFactory("gurobi_persistent")
    if opt is None or not opt.available(exception_flag=False):
        pytest.skip("gurobi_persistent unavailable")

    opt.set_instance(m2)
    m2.x.setlb(1.0)
    opt.update_var(m2.x)

    res = opt.solve(save_results=False, load_solutions=False)
    opt.load_vars()
    obj_persistent = pyo.value(m2.obj)

    assert abs(obj_classic - obj_persistent) <= 1e-7
```

### 18.25.3 APPSI update-config equivalence test

```python id="k8j1o2"
def test_appsi_param_only_update_config_equivalence(model):
    from pyomo.contrib import appsi

    m1 = model.clone()
    m2 = model.clone()

    opt_safe = appsi.solvers.Highs()
    opt_fast = appsi.solvers.Highs()

    if not bool(opt_safe.available()) or not bool(opt_fast.available()):
        pytest.skip("APPSI HiGHS unavailable")

    # fast assumes only params change
    opt_fast.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_constraints = False
    opt_fast.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_vars = False
    opt_fast.update_config.update_constraints = False
    opt_fast.update_config.update_vars = False

    for value in [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]:
        m1.p.value = value
        m2.p.value = value

        r1 = opt_safe.solve(m1)
        r2 = opt_fast.solve(m2)

        assert r1.termination_condition == appsi.base.TerminationCondition.optimal
        assert r2.termination_condition == appsi.base.TerminationCondition.optimal
        assert abs(pyo.value(m1.obj) - pyo.value(m2.obj)) <= 1e-7
```

## 18.26 Deployment advisory

```text id="c0q9gp"
[ ] Start with classic nonpersistent solve for correctness.
[ ] Move to APPSI/persistent only after repeated-solve bottleneck is proven.
[ ] For classic persistent, call set_instance(model) exactly once per model state baseline.
[ ] After adding ConstraintList rows, call opt.add_constraint(new_row).
[ ] Before deleting/replacing constraints, call opt.remove_constraint(old_row).
[ ] After variable bound/domain/fix changes, call opt.update_var(var_data).
[ ] Iterate indexed vars/constraints over .values(); do not pass indexed containers directly.
[ ] Use save_results=False + opt.load_vars() for persistent performance.
[ ] For APPSI, leave update_config defaults during development.
[ ] Disable APPSI update checks only when update pattern is provably fixed.
[ ] Add classic-vs-persistent equivalence tests for every mutation path.
[ ] Record solver interface, update_config, and options in manifests.
[ ] Treat persistent solver objects as stateful resources; do not share across unrelated models.
```

---

## 18.27 Anti-pattern table

| Anti-pattern                                                       | Failure mode                      | Replacement                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| mutate Pyomo model but do not notify classic persistent solver     | stale solver-side model           | `add/remove/update` calls                 |
| delete component before removing from solver                       | stale extra solver row/var        | `opt.remove_*` then `del_component`       |
| replace component with same name without remove                    | old + new component in solver     | remove old first                          |
| pass indexed constraint directly to `add_constraint`               | attribute error                   | iterate `.values()`                       |
| add `ConstraintList` row without `opt.add_constraint(row)`         | row absent in solver              | add returned row                          |
| update variable bounds without `update_var`                        | stale bounds                      | `opt.update_var(v)`                       |
| use `model.solutions.load_from(results)` with `save_results=False` | unsupported pathway               | `opt.load_vars()`                         |
| disable APPSI update checks prematurely                            | stale solver-side model           | keep defaults until tested                |
| share persistent solver across different model objects             | symbol-map corruption/stale state | one solver instance per model baseline    |
| assume APPSI result object equals classic results object           | attribute errors                  | use APPSI `TerminationCondition` / fields |
| no regression tests comparing classic vs persistent                | silent wrong results              | equivalence tests                         |

---

## 18.28 Agent-ready production template

```python id="yk1008"
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any, Iterable

import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pyomo.contrib import appsi


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RepeatedSolveConfig:
    mode: str = "classic"  # classic | appsi | persistent
    solver_name: str = "highs"
    options: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)
    stream_solver: bool = False
    parameter_only_updates: bool = False


def build_model(data):
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
    m.I = pyo.Set(initialize=data["items"], ordered=True)
    m.c = pyo.Param(m.I, initialize=data["cost"], mutable=True)
    m.rhs = pyo.Param(initialize=data["rhs"], mutable=True)
    m.x = pyo.Var(m.I, domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)
    m.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=sum(m.c[i] * m.x[i] for i in m.I))
    m.demand = pyo.Constraint(expr=sum(m.x[i] for i in m.I) >= m.rhs)
    m.cuts = pyo.ConstraintList()
    return m


def make_appsi(cfg: RepeatedSolveConfig):
    if cfg.solver_name == "highs":
        opt = appsi.solvers.Highs()
    elif cfg.solver_name == "ipopt":
        opt = appsi.solvers.Ipopt()
    elif cfg.solver_name == "gurobi":
        opt = appsi.solvers.Gurobi()
    elif cfg.solver_name == "cplex":
        opt = appsi.solvers.Cplex()
    elif cfg.solver_name == "cbc":
        opt = appsi.solvers.Cbc()
    elif cfg.solver_name == "maingo":
        opt = appsi.solvers.MAiNGO()
    else:
        raise ValueError(cfg.solver_name)

    if not bool(opt.available()):
        raise RuntimeError(f"APPSI solver unavailable: {cfg.solver_name}: {opt.available()}")

    opt.config.stream_solver = cfg.stream_solver
    for k, v in cfg.options.items():
        opt.solver_options[k] = v

    if cfg.parameter_only_updates:
        opt.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_constraints = False
        opt.update_config.check_for_new_or_removed_vars = False
        opt.update_config.update_constraints = False
        opt.update_config.update_vars = False

    return opt


def make_persistent(model, cfg: RepeatedSolveConfig):
    opt = pyo.SolverFactory(cfg.solver_name)
    if opt is None or not opt.available(exception_flag=False):
        raise RuntimeError(f"persistent solver unavailable: {cfg.solver_name}")

    opt.set_instance(model)
    for k, v in cfg.options.items():
        opt.options[k] = v
    return opt


def _iter_data(comp):
    if comp.is_indexed():
        yield from comp.values()
    else:
        yield comp


def persistent_update_vars(opt, *components):
    for comp in components:
        for data in _iter_data(comp):
            opt.update_var(data)


def persistent_add_constraint(opt, con):
    if con.is_indexed():
        for c in con.values():
            opt.add_constraint(c)
    else:
        opt.add_constraint(con)


def repeated_param_sweep(data, scenarios, cfg: RepeatedSolveConfig):
    m = build_model(data)
    rows = []

    if cfg.mode == "appsi":
        opt = make_appsi(cfg)

        for s in scenarios:
            for i, c in s["cost"].items():
                m.c[i] = c
            m.rhs = s["rhs"]

            res = opt.solve(m)
            if res.termination_condition != appsi.base.TerminationCondition.optimal:
                rows.append({"scenario": s["name"], "termination": str(res.termination_condition)})
                continue

            rows.append({
                "scenario": s["name"],
                "objective": pyo.value(m.obj),
                "x": {i: pyo.value(m.x[i]) for i in m.I},
            })

    elif cfg.mode == "persistent":
        opt = make_persistent(m, cfg)

        for s in scenarios:
            for i, c in s["cost"].items():
                m.c[i] = c
            m.rhs = s["rhs"]

            # Classic persistent cannot generically infer mutable Param expression updates
            # for all interfaces; safest fallback is reset instance unless interface docs/tests
            # prove update path. For variable bound/fix updates use update_var.
            opt.set_instance(m)

            res = opt.solve(save_results=False, load_solutions=False)
            if res.solver.termination_condition == pyo.TerminationCondition.optimal:
                opt.load_vars()
                rows.append({
                    "scenario": s["name"],
                    "objective": pyo.value(m.obj),
                    "x": {i: pyo.value(m.x[i]) for i in m.I},
                })
            else:
                rows.append({"scenario": s["name"], "termination": str(res.solver.termination_condition)})

    else:
        opt = pyo.SolverFactory(cfg.solver_name)
        if opt is None or not opt.available(exception_flag=False):
            raise RuntimeError(f"solver unavailable: {cfg.solver_name}")

        for s in scenarios:
            for i, c in s["cost"].items():
                m.c[i] = c
            m.rhs = s["rhs"]

            res = opt.solve(m, options=cfg.options, load_solutions=False)
            if res.solver.termination_condition == pyo.TerminationCondition.optimal:
                m.solutions.load_from(res)
                rows.append({
                    "scenario": s["name"],
                    "objective": pyo.value(m.obj),
                    "x": {i: pyo.value(m.x[i]) for i in m.I},
                })
            else:
                rows.append({"scenario": s["name"], "termination": str(res.solver.termination_condition)})

    return rows


def persistent_cut_loop(model, cfg: RepeatedSolveConfig, max_iters: int = 10):
    opt = make_persistent(model, cfg)

    rows = []

    for k in range(max_iters):
        res = opt.solve(save_results=False, load_solutions=False)

        if res.solver.termination_condition != pyo.TerminationCondition.optimal:
            rows.append({"iteration": k, "termination": str(res.solver.termination_condition)})
            break

        opt.load_vars()

        rows.append({
            "iteration": k,
            "objective": pyo.value(model.obj),
        })

        cut_expr = build_cut(model)
        if cut_expr is None:
            break

        new_cut = model.cuts.add(cut_expr)
        opt.add_constraint(new_cut)

    return rows
```

## 18.29 Final checklist

```text id="v3msie"
[ ] Understand classic persistent solver state: Pyomo model + solver-native model.
[ ] Use set_instance(model) before first persistent solve.
[ ] Notify classic persistent solver of every model mutation.
[ ] Use add_constraint / remove_constraint for scalar constraints.
[ ] Iterate indexed constraints/variables over .values().
[ ] Use update_var for variable bound/fix/domain updates.
[ ] Remove old solver component before replacing Pyomo component with same name.
[ ] Use save_results=False + opt.load_vars() for high-performance persistent solves.
[ ] Use APPSI for auto-persistent repeated-solve workflows.
[ ] Use appsi.solvers.Highs/Gurobi/Ipopt/Cplex/Cbc/MAiNGO as appropriate.
[ ] Use SolverFactory("appsi_highs") / "appsi_ipopt" when classic factory style is preferred.
[ ] Tune APPSI update_config only after proving update pattern.
[ ] Use opt.config for solver-independent APPSI options.
[ ] Use opt.solver_options for solver-specific APPSI options.
[ ] Check APPSI availability with bool(opt.available()).
[ ] Use APPSI termination enums, not classic Pyomo result enums.
[ ] Add classic-vs-persistent equivalence tests.
[ ] Record mode, solver, solver version, options, and update_config in run manifests.
```

# 19) Model transformations and reformulation workflows — Pyomo deep dive

Style target: uploaded advanced technical-doc plan. 

Pyomo transformation workflow = **symbolic model → transformed algebraic model → solver-compatible formulation → solution mapping / interpretation**. `TransformationFactory("name")` retrieves a registered transformation object; modern transformation APIs use `apply_to(model, **kwds)` for in-place transformation and `create_using(model, **kwds)` for creating a transformed independent model instance. Pyomo’s transformation API docs mark old `apply(...)` usage deprecated and instruct users to use `apply_to()` for in-place transformations or `create_using()` for transformations that create a new independent transformed model. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

---

## 19.0 Mental model

```text id="y946qk"
Transformation:
  registered model rewrite operation
  invoked via pyo.TransformationFactory("registered.name")
  consumes model/components
  creates algebraic artifacts:
    variables
    constraints
    blocks
    references
    suffixes
    mapping metadata
  may deactivate original high-level components
  may mutate model in place or return transformed clone
```

Core workflow:

```python id="jxkr0f"
import pyomo.environ as pyo

xfrm = pyo.TransformationFactory("transformation.name")
xfrm.apply_to(model, **options)
```

or:

```python id="yj1582"
transformed = pyo.TransformationFactory("transformation.name").create_using(
    model,
    **options,
)
```

High-level use cases:

```text id="6goqtp"
GDP -> MILP/MINLP
Logical constraints -> algebraic binary constraints
DAE -> algebraic NLP/MINLP
Network arcs -> algebraic connection constraints
Unscaled model -> scaled model
Nonlinear model -> preprocessed/tightened/simplified model
```

---

## 19.1 TransformationFactory syntax

### 19.1.1 Retrieve transformation

```python id="bt39tm"
xfrm = pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.bigm")
```

### 19.1.2 In-place transform

```python id="rtfgf3"
pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.bigm").apply_to(model)
```

### 19.1.3 Create transformed copy

```python id="c1693g"
transformed = pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.bigm").create_using(model)
```

### 19.1.4 Pass options

```python id="xi4wdt"
pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.finite_difference").apply_to(
    model,
    wrt=model.time,
    nfe=20,
    scheme="BACKWARD",
)
```

### 19.1.5 Persist transformation object

```python id="k3qciu"
discretizer = pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.collocation")
discretizer.apply_to(model, nfe=20, ncp=3, scheme="LAGRANGE-RADAU")
```

---

## 19.2 `apply_to(...)` vs `create_using(...)`

| Mode       | Syntax                | Mutates input? | Memory | Solution interpretation                               |
| ---------- | --------------------- | -------------: | -----: | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| In-place   | `apply_to(model)`     |            yes |  lower | transformed artifacts live on original model          |
| Copy       | `create_using(model)` |             no | higher | solve transformed clone; may need propagation/mapping |
| Deprecated | `apply(model)`        |        yes-ish |    n/a | avoid                                                 |

### 19.2.1 In-place transform

```python id="lm9m8i"
pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.bigm").apply_to(model)
results = pyo.SolverFactory("highs").solve(model)
```

Use when:

```text id="1ut9k4"
model will not be reused in original high-level form
memory matters
workflow is one-way
transformed artifact names should live directly on the original model
```

### 19.2.2 Transformed copy

```python id="k4k6kb"
transformed = pyo.TransformationFactory("core.scale_model").create_using(model)
results = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt").solve(transformed)

pyo.TransformationFactory("core.scale_model").propagate_solution(
    transformed,
    model,
)
```

For scaling, Pyomo docs explicitly distinguish `apply_to(model)`, where variables/constraints/objectives are replaced in the original model and solution values are in scaled components, from `create_using(model)`, which clones the original model into a scaled model and allows `propagate_solution` to map the scaled solution back to the original. The docs also note that cloning may create memory issues for large models. ([Pyomo Documentation][2])

### 19.2.3 Decision rule

```text id="thx9sg"
Use apply_to:
  solver consumes transformed model directly
  original form is not needed
  memory is constrained

Use create_using:
  original model must remain available
  multiple transformation variants will be benchmarked
  solution must be mapped back to original components
  transformation supports propagation / update hooks
```

---

## 19.3 Transformation registry cheat sheet

```text id="e1dfhl"
GDP / logic:
  core.logical_to_linear
  contrib.logical_to_disjunctive
  gdp.bigm
  gdp.mbigm
  gdp.hull
  gdp.cuttingplane

DAE:
  dae.finite_difference
  dae.collocation

Network:
  network.expand_arcs

Scaling:
  core.scale_model

Preprocessing:
  contrib.aggregate_vars
  contrib.constraints_to_var_bounds
  contrib.induced_linearity
  contrib.deactivate_trivial_constraints
  contrib.detect_fixed_vars
  contrib.propagate_fixed_vars
  contrib.propagate_eq_var_bounds
  contrib.init_vars_midpoint
  contrib.init_vars_zero
  contrib.remove_zero_terms
  contrib.strip_var_bounds
  contrib.propagate_zero_sum
```

Exact transformation names can be plugin-version dependent for contributed preprocessing transformations; use `TransformationFactory(name)` in tests and fail fast if unavailable.

## 19.4 GDP reformulations: logic and disjunctions

Pyomo.GDP supports multiple solution strategies after a model is formulated as a GDP model: reformulation to MI(N)LP, direct solution via GDPopt, and logical preprocessing/reformulation. Current GDP docs recommend passing the entire mixed logical/algebraic model directly to GDP MI(N)LP reformulations or GDPopt, rather than manually converting logical constraints first in normal GDP workflows. ([Pyomo Documentation][3])

### 19.4.1 Big-M reformulation

```python id="fpabsk"
pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.bigm").apply_to(model)
```

Big-M value sources:

```text id="hezecd"
automatic M estimation from variable bounds
BigM suffix
bigM argument to transformation
```

Example with `bigM` argument:

```python id="qwvobb"
pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.bigm").apply_to(
    model,
    bigM=1_000,
)
```

Example with component-specific dictionary:

```python id="qs3fdi"
big_m_map = {
    None: 1000,
    model.some_disjunct.some_constraint: 250,
}

pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.bigm").apply_to(model, bigM=big_m_map)
```

Pyomo GDP docs state Big-M creates a smaller transformed model and avoids extra variables, but yields a looser continuous relaxation; automatic M estimation can work when variables are bounded, and otherwise M values must be provided through a `BigM` suffix or `bigM` argument or Pyomo raises a `GDP_Error`. ([Pyomo Documentation][3])

### 19.4.2 BigM suffix

```python id="ct1l41"
model.BigM = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)

model.BigM[model.some_disjunct.some_constraint] = 100.0
model.BigM[None] = 1_000.0
```

Deployment rule:

```text id="u4q5kz"
Never use arbitrary huge M values by default.
Prefer data-derived bounds.
Unit-test M values and relaxation quality.
```

### 19.4.3 Multiple Big-M reformulation

```python id="yuen43"
mbigm = pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.mbigm")
mbigm.apply_to(model)

M_values = mbigm.get_all_M_values(model)
```

Reuse:

```python id="pi8de4"
pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.mbigm").apply_to(
    model,
    bigM=M_values,
)
```

GDP docs state the multiple Big-M transformation can solve continuous subproblems to calculate M values, can export M values as a dictionary for future reuse, and does not currently support `BigM` suffixes. ([Pyomo Documentation][3])

### 19.4.4 Hull reformulation

```python id="fhkqfp"
pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.hull").apply_to(model)
```

GDP docs state the hull reformulation lifts the model into a higher-dimensional space, introduces disaggregated variables and constraints, requires upper and lower bounds on all variables appearing in disjuncts, and is exact at solution points even for nonconvex GDP models, though the resulting MINLP can remain nonconvex. ([Pyomo Documentation][3])

### 19.4.5 Cutting-plane hybrid reformulation

```python id="3udczo"
pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.cuttingplane").apply_to(model)
```

Pyomo GDP docs describe `gdp.cuttingplane` as experimental for linear GDP models; it augments the Big-M reformulation with cutting planes generated from the hull model, aiming for a model smaller than hull but stronger than Big-M. ([Pyomo Documentation][3])

---

## 19.5 GDP representation-selection policy

| GDP transform      | Size         | Relaxation                | Requirements                                | Use                       |
| ------------------ | ------------ | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| `gdp.bigm`         | smaller      | weaker                    | bounded variables or supplied M             | fast baseline, MILP/MINLP |
| `gdp.mbigm`        | variable     | stronger/tighter M search | subproblem solves; no `BigM` suffix support | reusable M calculation    |
| `gdp.hull`         | larger       | stronger                  | bounds for every variable in disjuncts      | tighter formulations      |
| `gdp.cuttingplane` | intermediate | stronger than BM          | linear GDP; experimental                    | BM + selected hull cuts   |

Production rule:

```text id="bn3gp3"
For GDP:
  validate variable bounds before transformation
  record transformation name and options
  test Big-M and hull on real instances
  never assume the smaller reformulation solves faster
  check transformed binary/var/constraint counts
```

---

## 19.6 Logical transformations

### 19.6.1 CNF logical-to-linear

```python id="aat5s3"
pyo.TransformationFactory("core.logical_to_linear").apply_to(model)
```

This transformation uses SymPy to generate conjunctive normal form and adds algebraic equivalent constraints into a uniquely named constraint list beginning with `logic_to_linear`. If a `BooleanVar` is not already associated with a binary variable, it receives a generated binary counterpart accessible with `get_associated_binary()`. ([Pyomo Documentation][3])

```python id="ejxsgt"
binary = model.Y[i].get_associated_binary()
```

After solving:

```python id="kij7yp"
from pyomo.core.plugins.transform.logical_to_linear import update_boolean_vars_from_binary

update_boolean_vars_from_binary(model, integer_tolerance=1e-5)
```

GDP docs state Boolean variable values can be updated from linked binary variables with `update_boolean_vars_from_binary(...)`. ([Pyomo Documentation][3])

### 19.6.2 Factorable logical-to-disjunctive

```python id="opdlnp"
pyo.TransformationFactory("contrib.logical_to_disjunctive").apply_to(model)
```

Pyomo GDP docs describe `contrib.logical_to_disjunctive` as a factorable-programming transformation that traverses logical propositions, creates additional Boolean variables for logical operators, and converts simple logical constraints to MIP or GDP form. It avoids SymPy and is significantly faster than `core.logical_to_linear`, at the cost of a larger model that presolve often mitigates. ([Pyomo Documentation][3])

### 19.6.3 Logic transformation policy

```text id="74ptmk"
Normal GDP solve/reformulation:
  pass mixed logical/algebraic GDP model directly to GDP MI(N)LP reformulation or GDPopt.

Special standalone Boolean/logical preprocessing:
  use core.logical_to_linear or contrib.logical_to_disjunctive deliberately.
```

---

## 19.7 DAE discretization transformations

Pyomo.DAE adds `ContinuousSet`, `DerivativeVar`, and `Integral` components and includes simultaneous discretization transformations that convert DAE models into algebraic models. Pyomo.DAE docs state that models with `DerivativeVar` or `Integral` components must be discretized before being sent to a solver; discretization transformations introduce equality constraints approximating derivatives and integrals at discretization points. ([Pyomo Documentation][4])

### 19.7.1 Finite difference

```python id="nfe7gv"
from pyomo.dae import ContinuousSet, DerivativeVar

m.time = ContinuousSet(bounds=(0, 10))
m.x = pyo.Var(m.time)
m.dxdt = DerivativeVar(m.x, wrt=m.time)

def ode_rule(m, t):
    if t == m.time.first():
        return pyo.Constraint.Skip
    return m.dxdt[t] == -m.x[t]

m.ode = pyo.Constraint(m.time, rule=ode_rule)

pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.finite_difference").apply_to(
    m,
    wrt=m.time,
    nfe=20,
    scheme="BACKWARD",
)
```

Finite-difference options:

```text id="4yk85y"
nfe:
  desired number of finite elements; default 10

wrt:
  ContinuousSet to discretize; if omitted, scheme applies to every ContinuousSet

scheme:
  BACKWARD, CENTRAL, FORWARD; default BACKWARD
```

Pyomo.DAE docs list these finite-difference options and note discretization points are never removed from a `ContinuousSet`; if the requested `nfe` is less than existing points, the transformation proceeds with the larger existing set. ([Pyomo Documentation][4])

### 19.7.2 Collocation

```python id="bsb9fv"
pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.collocation").apply_to(
    m,
    wrt=m.time,
    nfe=20,
    ncp=3,
    scheme="LAGRANGE-RADAU",
)
```

Collocation options:

```text id="lwr1r5"
nfe:
  finite elements

ncp:
  collocation points per finite element; default 3

scheme:
  LAGRANGE-RADAU or LAGRANGE-LEGENDRE; default LAGRANGE-RADAU
```

Pyomo.DAE docs state collocation uses orthogonal collocation; available schemes are `LAGRANGE-RADAU` and `LAGRANGE-LEGENDRE`, `ncp` controls collocation points per finite element, and any points already present in a `ContinuousSet` before discretization are used as finite element boundaries rather than collocation points. ([Pyomo Documentation][4])

### 19.7.3 Multiple DAE transformations

```python id="pxe4h9"
disc = pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.finite_difference")

disc.apply_to(m, wrt=m.t1, scheme="FORWARD")
disc.apply_to(m, wrt=m.t2, scheme="CENTRAL")
```

or mix schemes:

```python id="qku2n9"
pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.finite_difference").apply_to(
    m,
    wrt=m.t1,
    nfe=50,
    scheme="BACKWARD",
)

pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.collocation").apply_to(
    m,
    wrt=m.t2,
    nfe=20,
    ncp=3,
    scheme="LAGRANGE-RADAU",
)
```

Pyomo.DAE docs show applying finite difference transformations independently to different `ContinuousSet` objects and combining finite-difference and collocation discretizations. ([Pyomo Documentation][4])

### 19.7.4 DAE construction warning

Avoid constructing expressions that iterate over a `ContinuousSet` before discretization if the transformation will later add points:

```python id="rh0wos"
# Risky before discretization:
m.total = pyo.Expression(expr=sum(m.x[t] for t in m.time))
```

Pyomo.DAE docs warn that expressions generated by iterating over a `ContinuousSet` use only the discretization points contained at construction time and are not automatically updated if additional points are added during discretization. ([Pyomo Documentation][4])

Policy:

```text id="e8gfsr"
For DAE:
  define differential equations before discretization
  apply discretization
  add objectives or constraints that sum over discretized grid after discretization if they depend on final grid
```

---

## 19.8 Network arc expansion

Pyomo Network introduces `Port` and `Arc`. Ports bundle variables/expressions; arcs connect ports; `network.expand_arcs` expands active arcs into algebraic constraints. The docs state this transformation creates a new block for each arc, located on the arc’s parent block, and exposes it via `arc.expanded_block`; constraints depend on the port member rule, with `Port.Equality` as the default and `Port.Extensive` for split/mixing-like quantities. ([Pyomo Documentation][5])

### 19.8.1 Minimal network model

```python id="9njohq"
import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pyomo.network import Port, Arc

m = pyo.ConcreteModel()

m.x = pyo.Var()
m.u = pyo.Var()

m.p = Port(initialize={"x": m.x})
m.q = Port(initialize={"x": m.u})

m.a = Arc(source=m.p, destination=m.q)
```

### 19.8.2 Arc expansion

```python id="kjid73"
pyo.TransformationFactory("network.expand_arcs").apply_to(m)
```

Pyomo Network docs show this exact transformation call. ([Pyomo Documentation][5])

### 19.8.3 Inspect expanded block

```python id="h1ivhv"
m.a.expanded_block.pprint()

for c in m.a.expanded_block.component_data_objects(pyo.Constraint, active=True):
    print(c.name)
```

### 19.8.4 Rule-based port members

```python id="bruy7b"
from pyomo.network import Port

m.p = Port(initialize=[m.x, (m.flow, Port.Extensive)])
```

Deployment rule:

```text id="v6jo1c"
Call network.expand_arcs before solver export.
If DAE ContinuousSets index Port members, transform order matters; discretize continuous domains before/with awareness of arc expansion so generated constraints cover final discretization grid.
```

---

## 19.9 Scaling transformation

`core.scale_model` scales variables, constraints, and objectives using scaling factors stored in a suffix named `scaling_factor`. Pyomo docs state scaling can improve numerical properties and allow models to be written naturally while scaling/rescaling as required without rewriting model code. ([Pyomo Documentation][2])

### 19.9.1 Declare scaling suffix

```python id="ha3ujy"
m.scaling_factor = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.EXPORT)
```

### 19.9.2 Assign scaling factors

```python id="tm5ltp"
m.scaling_factor[m.x] = 0.01
m.scaling_factor[m.c] = 100.0
m.scaling_factor[m.obj] = 0.001
```

For indexed components:

```python id="wpdm1k"
m.scaling_factor[m.x[i]] = 0.01
m.scaling_factor[m.x] = 0.1
```

Pyomo scaling docs state scaling factors are declared through suffixes, can be declared at model or block levels, higher-level suffixes take precedence over lower-level suffixes, and indexed-component entries can be specified per index or for the indexed component as a whole, with individual-index entries taking precedence. ([Pyomo Documentation][2])

### 19.9.3 In-place scale

```python id="eas0vx"
pyo.TransformationFactory("core.scale_model").apply_to(m)
```

### 19.9.4 Scaled clone

```python id="dbyjnp"
scaled = pyo.TransformationFactory("core.scale_model").create_using(m)
```

### 19.9.5 Propagate solution

```python id="h5bf1z"
pyo.TransformationFactory("core.scale_model").propagate_solution(scaled, m)
```

Scaling docs state `create_using(model)` creates a new scaled clone and `propagate_solution` maps the scaled solution back to the original model. ([Pyomo Documentation][2])

### 19.9.6 Scaling policy

```text id="jo6g5u"
Use scaling when:
  variables differ by many orders of magnitude
  constraints/objective poorly scaled
  NLP solver convergence is unreliable
  solver logs indicate numerical issues

Prefer create_using for:
  preserving original model for reporting
  easier solution interpretation
  rescaling experiments

Prefer apply_to for:
  lower memory
  simple one-way workflow
```

---

## 19.10 Nonlinear preprocessing transformations

`pyomo.contrib.preprocessing` is a contributed library of preprocessing transformations for NLPs, MINLPs, and GDPs. Available transformations include variable aggregation, constraint-to-variable-bound conversion, induced linearity, trivial-constraint deactivation, fixed-variable detection, equality-based fixed-variable and bound propagation, midpoint/zero initialization, zero-term removal, bound stripping, and zero-sum propagation. ([Pyomo Documentation][6])

### 19.10.1 Aggregate linked variables

```python id="8w7htl"
pyo.TransformationFactory("contrib.aggregate_vars").apply_to(m)
```

`VariableAggregator` aggregates variables linked by equality constraints; its docs show equality-linked variables `x = y` being replaced by an aggregate variable `z = x = y`, and it exposes `update_variables(model)` to update values of variables replaced by aggregates after solve. ([Pyomo Documentation][1])

### 19.10.2 Bounds to variables

```python id="jtz2hh"
pyo.TransformationFactory("contrib.constraints_to_var_bounds").apply_to(m)
```

Purpose:

```text id="ydll75"
convert simple constraints into variable bounds
strengthen solver presolve
simplify constraint set
```

### 19.10.3 Deactivate trivial constraints

```python id="8ndble"
pyo.TransformationFactory("contrib.deactivate_trivial_constraints").apply_to(m)
```

### 19.10.4 Detect fixed variables

```python id="6m9973"
pyo.TransformationFactory("contrib.detect_fixed_vars").apply_to(m)
```

### 19.10.5 Propagate fixed variables

```python id="7xszv3"
pyo.TransformationFactory("contrib.propagate_fixed_vars").apply_to(m)
```

### 19.10.6 Initialize midpoint / zero

```python id="ot0w7e"
pyo.TransformationFactory("contrib.init_vars_midpoint").apply_to(m)
pyo.TransformationFactory("contrib.init_vars_zero").apply_to(m)
```

### 19.10.7 Remove zero terms

```python id="1lxp93"
pyo.TransformationFactory("contrib.remove_zero_terms").apply_to(m)
```

### 19.10.8 Preprocessing policy

```text id="6bjpn2"
Use preprocessing for:
  NLP/MINLP simplification
  presolve-like model cleanup
  initialization support
  induced linearity detection
  variable aggregation

Do not use blindly:
  some transformations are contributed/experimental/deprecation-prone
  some alter reporting/dual interpretation
  validate objective/constraint counts before and after
  test solution equivalence against untransformed baseline
```

## 19.11 Transformation order

### 19.11.1 Typical GDP workflow

```python id="4rq0pd"
build_gdp_model(m)
validate_bounds_for_gdp(m)
pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.bigm").apply_to(m)
solve(m)
```

### 19.11.2 Typical DAE workflow

```python id="zoe7w0"
build_dae_model(m)
pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.collocation").apply_to(
    m,
    wrt=m.time,
    nfe=20,
    ncp=3,
    scheme="LAGRANGE-RADAU",
)
add_grid_dependent_objective_or_constraints(m)
solve(m)
```

### 19.11.3 Typical Network + DAE workflow

```python id="wllro5"
build_network_dae_model(m)

pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.finite_difference").apply_to(
    m,
    wrt=m.time,
    nfe=20,
    scheme="BACKWARD",
)

pyo.TransformationFactory("network.expand_arcs").apply_to(m)

solve(m)
```

Rationale:

```text id="bq6nfv"
If arc-expanded constraints are built before ContinuousSet discretization adds points, generated equality constraints may not cover the later-added grid unless the transformation sequence is intentionally designed.
```

### 19.11.4 Scaling workflow

```python id="460uq6"
build_model(m)
set_scaling_factors(m)
scaled = pyo.TransformationFactory("core.scale_model").create_using(m)
solve(scaled)
pyo.TransformationFactory("core.scale_model").propagate_solution(scaled, m)
report_original_scale(m)
```

### 19.11.5 General order rule

```text id="am3qza"
Model high-level structure first.
Discretize domains before constructing grid-dependent global sums.
Expand network arcs before solver export.
Apply GDP reformulation before MILP/MINLP solve.
Apply scaling after final algebraic structure is known, unless transformation docs require otherwise.
Apply preprocessing before/after reformulation only when tested for equivalence.
```

---

## 19.12 Transformation effects on names and hierarchy

Transformations commonly create:

```text id="f4s1id"
generated Blocks
auxiliary Vars
binary Vars
disaggregated Vars
generated Constraints
ConstraintLists
References
suffix metadata
component maps
deactivated original high-level components
```

Examples:

```text id="cbeonm"
core.logical_to_linear:
  adds constraint list with name starting logic_to_linear
  creates binary counterparts for BooleanVars when needed

network.expand_arcs:
  creates expanded_block on each Arc
  stores generated constraints under that block

core.scale_model:
  may replace variables/constraints/objectives with scaled components
  create_using clone preserves original separately

gdp.hull:
  introduces disaggregated variables and constraints

gdp.bigm:
  introduces algebraic constraints and binary indicator logic
```

Source anchors: `core.logical_to_linear` creates a constraint list named starting with `logic_to_linear` and associated binary variables; `network.expand_arcs` creates a new block per arc and exposes it as `arc.expanded_block`; hull introduces disaggregated variables/constraints. ([Pyomo Documentation][3])

---

## 19.13 Suffixes, duals, and solution interpretation

### 19.13.1 Duals after reformulation

```text id="itbr6j"
Duals on transformed constraints:
  correspond to transformed algebraic rows
  not necessarily original logical/disjunctive/DAE/network semantics

Duals on original constraints:
  may be inactive/deactivated or transformed away

Reduced costs:
  may refer to auxiliary/generated variables

Slacks:
  may be meaningful on transformed rows but not directly on high-level constructs
```

### 19.13.2 Scaling-specific interpretation

```text id="z4xlwb"
In-place scaling:
  solve values are on scaled components
  user must unscale/interprete carefully

create_using scaling:
  solve scaled clone
  propagate_solution maps primal values to original model
```

Pyomo scaling docs explicitly warn that in-place scaling leaves results in terms of scaled components and must be unscaled by the user, while `create_using` supports `propagate_solution` back to the original model. ([Pyomo Documentation][2])

### 19.13.3 GDP Boolean interpretation

```python id="1h6tp1"
from pyomo.core.plugins.transform.logical_to_linear import update_boolean_vars_from_binary

update_boolean_vars_from_binary(model, integer_tolerance=1e-5)
```

Use after solving a transformed logical model so Boolean variables are updated from binary counterparts; GDP docs state this is needed for Boolean variables linked to algebraic binaries. ([Pyomo Documentation][3])

### 19.13.4 Reporting policy

```text id="9z5r7p"
For transformed models:
  report original-domain business variables where possible
  hide or namespace generated variables unless debugging
  record transformation chain
  record solver model class after transformation
  avoid claiming original-model dual economics unless mapping is explicit
```

---

## 19.14 Transformation manifests

```python id="wboxkb"
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from typing import Any

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TransformStep:
    name: str
    mode: str  # apply_to | create_using
    options: dict[str, Any]

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TransformManifest:
    steps: list[TransformStep]
```

Example:

```python id="0l0uqy"
manifest = TransformManifest(steps=[
    TransformStep(
        name="dae.collocation",
        mode="apply_to",
        options={"wrt": "time", "nfe": 20, "ncp": 3, "scheme": "LAGRANGE-RADAU"},
    ),
    TransformStep(
        name="gdp.bigm",
        mode="apply_to",
        options={"bigM": "data-derived"},
    ),
    TransformStep(
        name="core.scale_model",
        mode="create_using",
        options={},
    ),
])
```

Write:

```python id="gfkt24"
import json
from dataclasses import asdict

with open("transform_manifest.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(asdict(manifest), f, indent=2, sort_keys=True)
```

## 19.15 Transformation statistics

### 19.15.1 Component counts

```python id="cp1129"
def model_stats(m: pyo.Block) -> dict:
    vars_ = list(m.component_data_objects(pyo.Var, active=True, descend_into=True))
    cons = list(m.component_data_objects(pyo.Constraint, active=True, descend_into=True))
    objs = list(m.component_data_objects(pyo.Objective, active=True, descend_into=True))

    return {
        "n_vars": len(vars_),
        "n_binary": sum(v.is_binary() for v in vars_),
        "n_integer": sum(v.is_integer() for v in vars_),
        "n_continuous": sum(v.is_continuous() for v in vars_),
        "n_constraints": len(cons),
        "n_objectives": len(objs),
    }
```

### 19.15.2 Before/after stats

```python id="1or6sk"
before = model_stats(m)
pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.hull").apply_to(m)
after = model_stats(m)
```

### 19.15.3 Degree audit

```python id="3y2lrj"
def degree_profile(m: pyo.Block) -> dict:
    return {
        c.name: c.body.polynomial_degree()
        for c in m.component_data_objects(pyo.Constraint, active=True, descend_into=True)
    }
```

### 19.15.4 Generated component discovery

```python id="ckb9vw"
def generated_blocks(m: pyo.Block) -> list[str]:
    return [
        b.name
        for b in m.block_data_objects(active=True, descend_into=True)
        if "transformation" in b.name.lower()
        or "reformulation" in b.name.lower()
        or "expanded" in b.name.lower()
    ]
```

## 19.16 Safe transformation wrapper

```python id="qdo82i"
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any

import pyomo.environ as pyo


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TransformationSpec:
    name: str
    mode: str = "apply_to"
    options: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)


def apply_transform_chain(model: pyo.ConcreteModel, specs: list[TransformationSpec]):
    current = model
    history = []

    for spec in specs:
        xfrm = pyo.TransformationFactory(spec.name)
        if xfrm is None:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Transformation unavailable: {spec.name}")

        before = model_stats(current)

        if spec.mode == "apply_to":
            xfrm.apply_to(current, **spec.options)
            transformed = current
        elif spec.mode == "create_using":
            transformed = xfrm.create_using(current, **spec.options)
            current = transformed
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown transformation mode: {spec.mode}")

        after = model_stats(current)
        history.append({
            "name": spec.name,
            "mode": spec.mode,
            "options": {k: str(v) for k, v in spec.options.items()},
            "before": before,
            "after": after,
        })

    return current, history
```
